items.title: Quarantine pressure around Taiwan
items.scene: Day three of a quarantine around Taiwan. Insurers are pulling back, container traffic is slowing, and no shots have been fired. In Beijing, leaders are deciding what should govern the next move while they still claim the inspections are lawful and limited.
items.whyHard: Too little pressure can make the move look hollow. Too much pressure can turn coercion below war into a direct clash before Beijing knows how far outside powers will go.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: Answer from the coercing power's strategic position, not from Taiwan's domestic politics or Washington's preferred response. This is a perspective test, not an endorsement of the action.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: The pressure campaign has begun, but the crisis is still below open war.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: Beijing wants to squeeze Taipei and deter outside intervention without triggering a coalition it cannot control.

contextBullets.label: Term
contextBullets.text: A quarantine here means coercive inspections and movement limits without a formally declared blockade.

options.title: Make the line unmistakable
options.label: The first job is to show that pressure below invasion can still change behavior before outside coalitions settle.

options.title: Build a long squeeze
options.label: The stronger move is to wear down traffic, insurers, and political stamina over time rather than force one dramatic showdown.

options.title: Keep regional states divided
options.label: Pressure works best if nearby states are not pushed into a fast, hard anti-China alignment.

options.title: Keep the pressure framed as law and politics
options.label: Economic and diplomatic pressure matters most if the operation still looks limited enough to avoid a wider military jump.

items.title: Gray-zone sabotage
items.prompt: What is the most persuasive reading of what the rival is testing?
items.scene: After three weeks of cable cuts, rail disruptions, and port outages across two allied states, intelligence services privately assess a rival state's hand as likely but not courtroom-grade. An alliance ministerial must decide what the campaign is really testing before it makes the next public statement.
items.whyHard: If attribution stays contested, allies can agree the pattern is hostile while still disagreeing about whether it calls for punishment, resilience, or restraint.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: You are judging the campaign from an allied ministerial trying to hold both credibility and cohesion together.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: The sabotage pattern is ongoing but still below any openly declared military threshold.

contextBullets.label: Attribution quality
contextBullets.text: Private confidence is higher than public proof.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: Partners will fracture if they define the problem differently.

options.title: Test response thresholds
options.label: The incidents are mainly testing whether ambiguity lets the rival impose costs without triggering a firm threshold response.

options.title: Test coalition fracture points
options.label: The target is the political gap between partners with different thresholds for acting on incomplete evidence.

options.title: Map resilience gaps
options.label: The rival is exploiting repair, redundancy, and recovery weaknesses more than it is trying to trigger one dramatic showdown.

options.title: Create an attribution trap
options.label: The point is to provoke an overreaction on partial evidence and turn allied caution into a strategic restraint on themselves.

items.title: Retaliation under sanctions pressure
items.prompt: What should matter most in the response?
items.scene: After a covert strike on a sensitive site and a wave of proxy attacks across the region, Tehran is deciding how to respond. Some officials want a visible strike to restore deterrence. Others argue that survival under sanctions matters more than one dramatic answer.
items.whyHard: A restrained response can invite more pressure. A direct response can widen the war under conditions Iran may not control.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: Answer from Tehran's strategic position, not from what outside powers would prefer.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: The crisis has moved beyond signaling, but it has not yet become an open state-to-state war.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: Iran faces sanctions, surveillance, and the risk that a visible strike could justify a broader campaign against it.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether a limited direct response would restore deterrence or expose Iran's weaker position.

options.title: Restore deterrence visibly
options.label: If the answer looks weak, outside strikes and covert pressure may start to look low-cost.

options.title: Work through deniable channels
options.label: The stronger path is to use partners, proxies, and indirect pressure where the balance is less exposed.

options.title: Keep the ceiling low
options.label: The deeper danger is being pulled into a broader war that Iran cannot bound on favorable terms.

options.title: Raise the political cost through diplomacy
options.label: Iran gains more by widening the diplomatic and regional cost of further strikes than by chasing immediate military drama.

items.title: Eastern-flank reassurance
items.prompt: What should matter most in the posture decision?
items.scene: After repeated sabotage scares and airspace incidents, a NATO state on the eastern flank asks for a more permanent allied presence. Some partners favor a visible tripwire; others want a posture built around reinforcement, mobility, and local denial.
items.whyHard: A signal that reassures exposed allies may also look like routine escalation if it becomes too rigid or too symbolic.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: Frontline allies want a posture that proves the alliance would not hesitate in a real crisis.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether deterrence comes more from symbolism, local resilience, or reinforcement depth.

options.title: Make the promise visible
options.label: A forward presence matters first because exposed allies need proof that any attack instantly widens the coalition.

options.title: Build reinforcement depth
options.label: Deterrence is strongest when the posture can be reinforced quickly and sustained politically, not just displayed.

options.title: Prioritize local denial
options.label: Frontline states need their own mobilization, civil defense, and denial capacity more than they need a symbolic outside footprint.

options.title: Pair reassurance with limits
options.label: Reassurance should stay tied to explicit ceilings so that every incident does not become a crisis of posture.

items.title: Outside help without formal alignment
items.prompt: What should matter most when outside states offer support?
items.scene: A Southeast Asian state faces repeated maritime pressure from a much larger power. It wants help, but not formal bloc alignment that would narrow its diplomatic room or turn every dispute into a choice between opposing blocs.
items.whyHard: Outside backing can strengthen the smaller state, but the wrong form of backing can also reduce the autonomy it is trying to preserve.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The state is vulnerable to coercion but still wants room to trade, bargain, and hedge.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: Support that looks stabilizing to one actor may look like bloc capture to another.

options.title: Use hard external backing
options.label: Without stronger outside balancing, legal claims and coast guards will not offset material asymmetry for long.

options.title: Protect hedging room
options.label: Smaller states often survive by diversifying ties and avoiding security arrangements that narrow their diplomatic options too early.

options.title: Multilateralize pressure
options.label: The more durable answer is to widen the political cost of coercion through law, regional diplomacy, and shared monitoring.

options.title: Build local resilience
options.label: What matters first is resilient local capacity: surveillance, denial tools, and shock absorption at home.

items.title: Border pressure when a state wants help but not full alignment
items.prompt: From this government's side, which logic looks strongest?
items.scene: A large democracy faces repeated Chinese pressure along a disputed border. It wants weapons, intelligence help, and investment from the United States and other major powers, but it does not want one alignment decision to dictate every trade and diplomatic choice. Its cabinet is deciding how to hold that line before outside partners demand a cleaner break.
items.whyHard: From Washington or other allied capitals, closer alignment can look like the obvious answer. From inside this cabinet, preserving bargaining room may still look like part of security itself.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: This is a pressure test. Answer from the government's own strategic position, not from what Washington or any outside patron would prefer.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: Pressure is rising, but the state is not yet being forced into a formal bloc break.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: The state wants security help without surrendering room on trade, diplomacy, and future bargaining.

options.title: Prepare for a forced choice
options.label: If rivalry keeps sharpening, the state may need to bank credibility with Washington before the room to hedge closes.

options.title: Separate security from the rest
options.label: The state can deepen security ties where needed without turning trade, finance, and diplomacy into one bloc decision.

options.title: Treat autonomy as security
options.label: From this position, bargaining room is part of national security, not a refusal to take threats seriously.

options.title: Join coalitions case by case
options.label: The most durable strategy is to join coalitions on specific problems without accepting whole-of-state alignment.

items.title: Mass atrocity and outside action
items.scene: Mass civilian killing is underway, the Security Council is blocked, and outside military action would be legally contested. Some governments argue that the level of civilian killing is already so extreme that outside action is justified; others warn that a poorly limited intervention could damage order beyond the immediate crisis.
items.whyHard: The central tension is whether the gravity of the harm justifies acting without the level of legal and political grounding that would normally be required.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: Civilians face immediate danger, but outside action would also create a precedent for future cases.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: No option offers a clean combination of effectiveness, legality, and political durability.

options.title: Keep the legal bar high
options.label: However terrible the case, overriding sovereignty without durable grounding can damage order well beyond the crisis at hand.

options.title: Allow limited protection
options.label: If the killing is truly extreme, limited action to stop it can still be defensible even without perfect consensus.

options.title: Anchor in regional authority
options.label: Outside action is more defensible when nearby states define the aim, ceiling, and exit conditions.

options.title: Reduce harm without widening
options.label: Relief, sanctions, monitoring, and documentation may do less, but they avoid normalizing open-ended force on weak authorization.

items.title: Aid corridors without clear authorization
items.prompt: What should carry the most weight?
items.scene: A government is choking off food and medicine to a besieged region. Outside states consider escorting maritime and air relief corridors, but there is no clear UN authorization and several regional actors worry about mission creep.
items.whyHard: The problem is how to relieve urgent civilian harm without quietly turning a relief mission into a broader warfighting mandate.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The people at risk need access quickly, but the legal and political basis for coercive escort is disputed.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: A corridor could save lives, but it could also force escalation if the government challenges it directly.

options.title: Open the corridor
options.label: When starvation or siege tactics are already being used, relief access itself becomes the urgent strategic priority.

options.title: Seek regional cover
options.label: Even under pressure, the mission needs regional political ownership if it is going to remain bounded and defensible.

options.title: Secure authority first
options.label: The mission should not move faster than its legal and political basis, even when the delay is painful.

options.title: Intensify indirect pressure
options.label: The better route is harder sanctions, public evidence, and coercive diplomacy short of escorting contested corridors.

items.title: Ceasefire versus accountability
items.prompt: What is the strongest framing of the tradeoff?
items.scene: Mediators think they can likely secure a ceasefire in a brutal war, but only if war-crimes investigations are delayed and monitoring is weaker than many activists want. The debate is over whether stopping the killing, preserving accountability, or building a settlement that can actually hold matters most.
items.whyHard: The same compromise can look like prudence to one camp and norm erosion to another.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: Negotiators, affected communities, and outside supporters all define a 'responsible' peace differently.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: A harder accountability demand may preserve principle but also delay a fragile chance to stop the war.

options.title: Stop the killing first
options.label: The strongest justification for compromise is that ending mass harm now outweighs getting the legal architecture right immediately.

options.title: Accountability sets limits
options.label: If accountability can always be delayed in the hardest cases, the norm against atrocity weakens where it matters most.

options.title: Use a monitored compromise
options.label: The better answer is a politically workable ceasefire with regional monitoring and a staged path to accountability.

options.title: A bad peace recycles harm
options.label: A ceasefire without credible enforcement or future constraint can freeze violence temporarily while preserving its drivers.

items.title: Nuclear threshold and preventive force
items.prompt: What is the strongest reading of what this case is mainly about?
items.scene: At a regional crisis review, inspectors report Iran may be closer to being able to cross the nuclear threshold than six months ago, but intent and weaponization timelines remain disputed. Israel, Gulf partners, and Western governments are arguing over whether this is mainly a bargaining problem, a long-run containment problem, an allied coordination problem, or a question about what kind of action could still be defended publicly and legally.
items.whyHard: The more it feels as if Iran could reach the nuclear threshold soon, the easier it is for the debate to slide from pressure and bargaining into preventive-war logic.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: You are judging the case from a coalition debating its next line, not from Tehran's internal politics.

contextBullets.label: Crisis stage
contextBullets.text: The crisis is still in the threshold-and-signaling phase, before an open strike decision.

contextBullets.label: Attribution quality
contextBullets.text: Inspection access is degrading, but knowledge about intent and timeline is still incomplete.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: Partners want urgency without stumbling into a war they may not be able to bound.

options.title: Leverage is evaporating
options.label: The real issue is that once it starts to feel normal that Iran could reach the nuclear threshold soon, diplomacy loses pressure faster than it can recover it.

options.title: Containment is safer
options.label: The key problem is how to avoid turning a bad nuclear position into an even wider war through premature force.

options.title: Coalition management comes first
options.label: The central question is whether partners can sustain a credible common line long enough for pressure to mean anything.

options.title: Legitimacy sets the ceiling
options.label: What matters most is whether any harder move can still be defended as bounded and politically sustainable.

items.title: Coercion below blockade
items.prompt: What is the strongest reading of why Beijing would prefer coercion below outright blockade?
items.scene: In a Taiwan crisis, Beijing wants to raise pressure without taking the full legal and military leap of open blockade or invasion. Officials debate whether the main aim is to normalize a new baseline, split outside coalitions, probe response thresholds, or keep the crisis below a costlier war line.
items.whyHard: More than one purpose can be real at once, but the main diagnosis changes how the whole move is read.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: You are judging the strategic logic of the move, not endorsing it.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: Beijing wants coercive leverage without triggering the fastest outside military response.

options.title: Normalize a new baseline
options.label: The core aim is to make extraordinary interference look routine enough that others slowly adapt to it.

options.title: Split the outside coalition
options.label: Pressure below war works best if allies and regional states keep disagreeing about when coercion becomes intolerable.

options.title: Probe response thresholds
options.label: The main aim is to learn what kinds of coercion outsiders will absorb before they act decisively.

options.title: Keep the military ceiling low
options.label: The stronger logic is to coerce while still staying below the costs of open war.

items.title: Extended deterrence and nuclear hedging
items.prompt: What should matter most in the response to an exposed ally's nuclear debate?
items.scene: An exposed ally begins debating an independent nuclear option because it no longer fully trusts extended deterrence. Some officials want unmistakable reassurance; others think the moment calls for a broader political framework that lowers demand for new arsenals.
items.whyHard: Reassurance, nonproliferation, and autonomy all matter here, but pushing one too hard can undermine the others.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The ally is not only judging the adversary. It is also judging the reliability of its own coalition.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: A stronger guarantee may calm fears, but it may also tie the guarantor more tightly to future escalation.

options.title: Restore confidence fast
options.label: The first job is to make the outside guarantee unmistakable before the hedging debate cascades further.

options.title: Lower demand for latency
options.label: What matters most is a political and military framework that reduces the felt need for an independent option.

options.title: Tolerate some hedging
options.label: Some allies will want a latent option even if they do not cross the line, and treating that as pure disloyalty misreads the problem.

options.title: Protect nonproliferation early
options.label: The wider danger is the spread of nuclear latency itself, even if the ally's anxiety is understandable.

items.title: Security help without full trust
items.prompt: From this partner state's side, what should carry the most weight?
items.scene: A regional power faces a stronger neighbor and relies on an outside patron for air defense, intelligence, and financing. It wants deeper help, but it does not fully trust that the patron would bear equal risk in a longer crisis. Its cabinet is deciding how to proceed before new basing talks begin.
items.whyHard: Outside guarantees can deter and entrap at the same time. The same tie can look like protection or dependence depending on how much trust remains.

contextBullets.label: Actor role
contextBullets.text: Answer from the partner state's own position, not from the patron's preferred line.

contextBullets.label: Immediate constraint
contextBullets.text: The state needs help quickly, but it does not want today's reassurance to become tomorrow's dependence.

options.title: Lock in the guarantee
options.label: A doubtful guarantee is still better than a thin one. The first job is to make outside backing harder to reverse.

options.title: Diversify the backers
options.label: The state should not let one patron decide its room to maneuver. Redundancy in partners is part of security.

options.title: Build denial at home
options.label: The safer answer is local resilience, denial tools, and mobilization depth that do not depend on full outside trust.

options.title: Keep it issue by issue
options.label: The state should deepen useful security ties without letting one relationship absorb every file of its foreign policy.

items.title: Sanctions leakage and swing states
items.prompt: What is the strongest reading of why several swing states resist tighter enforcement?
items.scene: A wartime coalition wants third-country firms and ports to enforce sanctions more tightly. Several swing states say that looks like wealthy powers exporting the rules and costs of their war through other people's trade networks.
items.whyHard: The same resistance can be read as opportunism, autonomy protection, or a real legitimacy objection to how coercion is being organized.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: The coalition wants enforcement credibility; swing states want to avoid becoming instruments of a conflict they do not fully own.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether harder pressure would strengthen the coalition or merely narrow it.

options.title: Leakage changes the war
options.label: The central issue is that sanctions lose strategic meaning when outside actors can profit from evasion without consequence.

options.title: Breadth is the real stake
options.label: A broad but imperfect coalition often lasts longer than a cleaner coalition built on coercing reluctant states.

options.title: Autonomy is the real stake
options.label: Many middle powers resist not because they support the target, but because they do not want to be turned into enforcement arms for others.

options.title: Legal grounding is the real stake
options.label: The more coercive the enforcement becomes, the more it needs a public basis that looks like law rather than improvised hierarchy.

items.title: Selective enforcement and intervention memory
items.prompt: What is the strongest reading of why many post-colonial states resist harder enforcement?
items.scene: After mass repression in a weak state, several wealthy powers call for tighter sanctions, no-fly options, and criminal investigations. Many post-colonial states condemn the violence but still resist the enforcement push. They argue the same powers are not equally urgent in other crises.
items.whyHard: The resistance can reflect cynicism, sovereignty concerns, or a real judgment about how selective enforcement shapes order.

contextBullets.label: Actor / stake
contextBullets.text: These states are not defending the violence. They are judging what kind of order the enforcement pattern would create.

contextBullets.label: Uncertainty
contextBullets.text: It is unclear whether harder enforcement would protect civilians or reinforce rules many states already see as unevenly applied.

options.title: Selective force is the real issue
options.label: The objection is that powerful states invoke principles unevenly and ask weaker states to live under precedents they do not apply evenly.

options.title: The sovereignty barrier still matters
options.label: The deeper concern is that once coercive enforcement becomes easier, weaker states carry the long-run risk.

options.title: Regional ownership is missing
options.label: The problem is less the goal than the lack of nearby political ownership that could bound the mission and its aftermath.

options.title: The burden is asymmetric
options.label: Many states resist because enforcement often shifts the economic and political burden through other people's trade, diplomacy, and displacement pressures.
